subject: ENG
label: Grade 03
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 03 English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 8 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Reading stories and poems
modules.outcome: read a story or poem and say the main idea and favourite part
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Reading stories and poems', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read a story or poem and say the main idea and favourite part. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Reading stories and poems' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read a story or poem and say the main idea and favourite part, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: cat, hat and mat rhyme. Make a couplet: 'The sun is high, a bird can fly.' High and fly rhyme. Method: Model run for 'Reading stories and poems'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read a story or poem and say the main idea and favourite part: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Read the story in order. Short text (my own): "Mina found a tiny boat on the shore. She pushed it into the stream. It sailed away, and she waved goodbye." Notice the three actions in order.
Step 2, State the main idea in one sentence. "Mina sends a small boat down a stream." Reason: the main idea is what the whole text is about, not every detail.
Step 3, Pick the favourite part and give a reason. "My favourite part is when the boat sails away because I like to imagine where it goes." Reason: always use "because" after your choice.
Step 4, Use evidence from the text. Question: "How did Mina feel?" Answer: "She felt happy because she waved goodbye." Reason: a clue from the text supports your answer.
Step 5, Fix an error. Weak main idea: "A boat." Better: "A girl sends a boat down a stream." Another error: "I like it because it is good." Better: "I like it because the boat sails far."
Step 6, Read a poem aloud. Lines (my own): "Rain on the roof, tap-tap-tap, / Cat on the mat, nap-nap-nap." Notice repeated sounds and rhyme: tap and nap. Reason: sound patterns make a poem fun.

Step 7, Your turn. Read: "A fox saw a grape on a high vine. He jumped and jumped but could not reach it." State the main idea and your favourite part. Model answer: "A fox tries to reach a grape. I like the jumping because it is funny."

modules.title: Subject and predicate
modules.outcome: find who or what a sentence is about and what it says about it
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Subject and predicate', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: find who or what a sentence is about and what it says about it. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Subject and predicate' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: find who or what a sentence is about and what it says about it, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'The tall boy | kicked the ball.' Subject: the tall boy. Predicate: kicked the ball. Method: Model run for 'Subject and predicate'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Find who or what a sentence is about and what it says about it: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Find the subject. Sentence: "The small bird sings." Ask: "Who or what sings?" Answer: "The small bird." That is the subject, the person or thing the sentence is about.

Step 2, Find the predicate. The rest, "sings", says what the subject does. In "The small bird sings in the tree", the predicate is "sings in the tree". Reason: the predicate tells what the subject does or is.
Step 3, Split sentences with a line. "My brother / plays football." "The big red bus / stopped at the corner." Subject on the left, predicate on the right. Reason: every full sentence has both.
Step 4, Spot an incomplete sentence. "Running down the hill." This has no subject. Fix: "The boys were running down the hill." Reason: a sentence needs a subject and a predicate.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The tall girl." Right: "The tall girl waved." Also check: "Waved to her friend." Right: "She waved to her friend."
Step 6, Practise with a longer sentence. "Our new teacher reads stories every Friday." Subject: "Our new teacher". Predicate: "reads stories every Friday." Check each part by asking who and what.
Step 7, Your turn. Divide this: "The cold wind blew through the window." Model answer: subject: "The cold wind"; predicate: "blew through the window."

modules.title: Nouns, pronouns and adjectives
modules.outcome: use them correctly and for variety
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Nouns, pronouns and adjectives', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: use them correctly and for variety. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Nouns, pronouns and adjectives' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: use them correctly and for variety, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: In 'Mira has a dog called Bruno', 'dog' is a common noun, 'Mira' and 'Bruno' are proper nouns and need capital letters. Method: Model run for 'Nouns, pronouns and adjectives'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Use them correctly and for variety: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Choose a pronoun to replace a noun. "Sara has a bag. She carries it to school." "Sara" becomes "she" and "bag" becomes "it". Reason: pronouns avoid repeating nouns.
Step 2, Use the right pronoun form. I/me, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them. Model: "Rafi and I went home." "The teacher gave him a book." Subject: I. Object: me. Test by removing the other name.
Step 3, Choose an adjective for more detail. Instead of "a dog", write "a friendly, brown dog". Nouns: dog. Adjectives: friendly, brown. Reason: adjectives tell what kind or which one.

Step 4, Vary your sentences. Weak: "The cat is big. The cat is soft. The cat is white." Better: "The cat is big, soft and white." Or: "It is a big, soft, white cat." Reason: variety keeps the reader interested.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Me and him went to the park." Right: "He and I went to the park." Another error: "Their going home." Right: "They're going home." (They are.)

Step 6, Rewrite a paragraph with pronouns. Before: "Ali likes cricket. Ali plays cricket on Monday." After: "Ali likes cricket. He plays it on Monday." Reason: he replaces Ali and it replaces cricket.
Step 7, Your turn. Rewrite using pronouns and one adjective: "Mum made a cake. Mum put the cake on the table." Model answer: "Mum made a delicious cake. She put it on the table."

modules.title: Verbs and simple tenses
modules.outcome: use present, past and future verbs correctly
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Verbs and simple tenses', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: use present, past and future verbs correctly. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Verbs and simple tenses' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: use present, past and future verbs correctly, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'The girl runs.' Add describing words: 'The tall girl runs fast.' Tense: walk, walked, will walk. Method: Model run for 'Verbs and simple tenses'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Use present, past and future verbs correctly: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Use the present for what is true now. "She walks to school." "The sun rises in the east." Add -s for he, she, it. Reason: the present simple names habits and facts.
Step 2, Use the past for what has finished. "She walked to school yesterday." Regular verbs end in -ed. Irregular: go, went; see, saw; make, made. Reason: the past tells what already happened.
Step 3, Use will for the future. "She will walk to school tomorrow." Or "going to": "She is going to walk." Reason: the future talks about things that have not happened yet.

Step 4, Keep tenses together. Right: "Yesterday we went to the market and bought mangoes." Wrong: "Yesterday we went to the market and buy mangoes." Reason: all actions in the same time need the same tense.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "He runned fast." Right: "He ran fast." Another error: "She will goes tomorrow." Right: "She will go tomorrow." After will, the verb stays plain.
Step 6, Change one sentence through three tenses. Present: "I paint a picture." Past: "I painted a picture." Future: "I will paint a picture." Mark the time word: now, yesterday, tomorrow.
Step 7, Your turn. Write "The children play cricket" in past and future. Model answer: past: "The children played cricket." Future: "The children will play cricket."

modules.title: Poetry and nonsense verse
modules.outcome: read limericks, notice rhyme and rhythm and write one
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Poetry and nonsense verse', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read limericks, notice rhyme and rhythm and write one. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Poetry and nonsense verse' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read limericks, notice rhyme and rhythm and write one, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Invent words but keep the rhythm: 'The wobbly wug went jig-a-jog, and hopped across the sleepy bog.' Jog and bog rhyme; four beats a line. Method: Model run for 'Poetry and nonsense verse'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read limericks, notice rhyme and rhythm and write one: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Notice rhyme in a limerick (my own): "A baker named Dee made a pie, / It was tall and it touched the sky; / The cat took a bite, / And flew off in fright, / And the baker just waved goodbye." Rhyme scheme: A A B B A.
Step 2, Find the rhythm. Lines one, two and five are longer, with about three beats; lines three and four are shorter, with two beats. Clap: "A BAK-er named DEE made a PIE." Reason: limericks bounce.

Step 3, Pick the nonsense. The sky is touched by a pie and a cat flies off. Nonsense verse uses silly ideas, invented words and surprising events. Reason: the humour comes from impossible events told seriously.

Step 4, Plan your limerick. Choose a name and a rhyme: "Jack" rhymes with "back", "sack", "snack". Idea: Jack carries a snack. Write line one: "A boy who was called Jack..." Reason: the first line sets the rhyme.
Step 5, Write all five lines. "A boy who was called Jack / Packed a snack in his sack; / A bee came to stay, / And ate it all day, / So he went home with nothing in his pack." Check rhyme A A B B A.

Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: "A boy who was called Jack / Took a snack in his park." Park does not rhyme with Jack. Right: "Took a snack in his sack." Choose words that really rhyme, not words only close in sound.
Step 7, Your turn. Write a limerick opening line and the rhyming second line about a goat named Moe. Model answer: "A goat who was named Moe / Wore a hat from head to toe," (Moe and toe rhyme).

modules.title: Speaking and listening
modules.outcome: give a one-minute talk and ask a question about a talk
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Speaking and listening', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: give a one-minute talk and ask a question about a talk. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Speaking and listening' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: give a one-minute talk and ask a question about a talk, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Retell in order with first, next, then, last. Ask: 'What happened next?' Reply politely: 'Thank you, I agree because...' Method: Model run for 'Speaking and listening'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Give a one-minute talk and ask a question about a talk: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Plan a one-minute talk with three parts. Topic: "My pet fish". Beginning: "I'd like to tell you about my fish." Middle: two facts. End: "Thank you for listening." Reason: three parts keep the talk clear.
Step 2, Write key words, not the full text. Cue card: "fish - Bubbles - orange - eats flakes - swims round." Reason: key words keep your eyes up and your voice natural.

Step 3, Speak at a steady pace. Model opening: "Good morning, everyone. I'd like to tell you about my fish, Bubbles." Count about 130 words per minute for a one-minute talk. Reason: a steady pace helps people follow.
Step 4, Add one interesting detail. "Bubbles is orange, and she always swims to the top when she hears my voice." Reason: a personal detail makes your talk memorable.
Step 5, Ask a question about a talk. "Why did you choose the name Bubbles?" "How often do you feed her?" Reason: a question must be about what the speaker said.
Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: speaking too fast and not looking up. Right: slow down and pause after each idea. Another weak question: "Is that all?" Better: "What does your fish eat?"
Step 7, Your turn. Prepare a 4-line cue card on "My favourite game" and one question to ask. Model answer: "game: football; friends; weekends; goal." Question: "How many players are on a team?"

ladder: L1: say and read familiar words and short sentences.
L2: read short texts and write connected sentences.
L3: write paragraphs and speak on a topic with notes.
L4: write for different purposes and analyse how texts persuade.
L5: write and argue at length; handle unseen texts.
L6 (degree): academic reading, writing and citation.
L7 (postgraduate): publish, teach or translate with expert accuracy.
